objectives: Map persistent organic pollutants (POPs) + DDT + dioxins + PCBs + PFAS + microplastics.
Apply bioaccumulation + biomagnification + LC50 in ecotoxicology.
Reason about PM2.5 + lead + arsenic + radon + asbestos + glyphosate + air-water pollutants.

slides.title: Persistent organic pollutants (POPs): DDT, dioxins, PCBs, PFAS, microplastics
slides.body:
**Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs)** — synthetic organic chemicals with four properties making them dangerous at population + ecosystem scale: (1) **persistence** (resist degradation; half-lives of years-decades in environment + tissue); (2) **bioaccumulation** (lipophilic + sequestered in adipose tissue); (3) **long-range transport** (semi-volatile; 'grasshopper' global distillation toward polar regions; Wania + Mackay); (4) **toxicity** (often endocrine, developmental, carcinogenic, immunotoxic). The **Stockholm Convention on POPs (2001; entered into force 2004)** is the international treaty controlling them — initially the 'Dirty Dozen,' now ~30 substances.

**DDT (dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane)** — synthesized 1874 (Zeidler); insecticidal property discovered by Paul Müller 1939 (Nobel 1948). WWII deployment + global malaria + typhus control. By 1962, **Rachel Carson's Silent Spring** documented bird-population collapse (eggshell thinning from DDE — the major DDT metabolite — inhibiting carbonic anhydrase + calcium deposition; bald eagle, peregrine falcon, brown pelican); persistent residues in food chain; growing concern for human health (suspected breast cancer link, developmental). Banned in US 1972 (EPA's first major regulatory action under William Ruckelshaus); Stockholm POP 2001. **Status today**: DDT still used (restricted) for indoor residual spraying against malaria vectors under WHO endorsement — the Stockholm Convention permits this for public health where alternatives insufficient. Tradeoff between immediate malaria mortality + chronic ecological/health effects.

**Dioxins (TCDD = 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin)** — unintentional by-products of combustion (incinerators, forest fires) + chlorinated chemistry (PVC, paper bleaching, herbicide synthesis). 75 PCDD + 135 PCDF + 209 PCB congeners — TEF (Toxic Equivalency Factor) system normalizes to TCDD potency. Mechanism: **aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR)** ligand → transcriptional reprogramming → chloracne, hepatic enzyme induction, immune suppression, developmental + reproductive toxicity, carcinogenesis (IARC Group 1). Half-life in humans ~7-11 years (adipose storage; slow elimination). Major incidents: **Seveso (1976, Italy)** — ICMESA plant explosion released TCDD over Brianza; chloracne cases + decades of cancer + immune followup (Mocarelli, Bertazzi). **Times Beach Missouri (1971-1983)** — Russell Bliss sprayed dioxin-contaminated oil on roads; EPA evacuated the town. **Agent Orange** (Vietnam) — 2,4,5-T herbicide contaminated with TCDD (Operation Ranch Hand); Vietnamese + US veterans elevated cancer + birth-defect rates. **Yusho (Japan 1968) + Yu-Cheng (Taiwan 1979)** — PCB-contaminated rice oil with PCDF impurities; long-term developmental cohort followup (Rogan + Hsu).

**PCBs (polychlorinated biphenyls)** — industrial dielectrics + plasticizers + heat-transfer fluids; Monsanto Aroclor brands. Mass-produced 1929-1979. Banned US 1979 (TSCA's first major chemical ban) + Stockholm POP 2001. Persistence: half-lives decades; ubiquitous in environment + tissue. **Anniston Alabama** Monsanto plant + Hudson River GE plant — landmark contamination cases + EPA superfund cleanups. Toxicity: dioxin-like (coplanar congeners, AhR), endocrine + neurodevelopmental + carcinogenic. Faroe Islands cohort (Grandjean + Weihe) linked prenatal PCB + Hg from whale meat to cognitive deficit.

**PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances)** — 'forever chemicals'; carbon-fluorine bond extreme stability (~480 kJ/mol). Mass family includes **PFOA (Teflon precursor), PFOS (Scotchgard), GenX, ADONA**, ~12000+ structures. Uses: nonstick cookware, water/stain-repellent textiles + paper, firefighting AFFF foam, cosmetics, food packaging, medical devices. Global contamination: detected in serum of >99% of US population (CDC NHANES; Calafat); contamination of drinking water (DuPont/3M Parkersburg WV — Bilott litigation; military bases with AFFF training). Half-life in humans: PFOS ~5.4 y, PFOA ~3.5 y, PFHxS ~8.5 y. Toxicity: developmental + immune (reduced vaccine antibody response — Grandjean Faroe cohort) + thyroid + cholesterol + kidney + testicular cancer. Stockholm: PFOS (2009), PFOA (2019), PFHxS (2022). EPA MCL for PFOA + PFOS set at 4 ppt (parts per trillion) 2024 — among most stringent drinking-water standards ever. Litigation: 3M $10.3B settlement 2023; DuPont/Chemours/Corteva; product reformulation underway.

**Microplastics + nanoplastics** — fragments <5 mm (micro) and <1 μm (nano) from textile fiber shedding, tire wear, plastic-product degradation, primary microbeads. Detected in food (seafood, salt, water), drinking water, air, human placenta, blood, lung tissue. Health effects emerging: oxidative stress + inflammation + endocrine activity (plasticizer additives — BPA, phthalates); 'Trojan horse' adsorption of POPs onto particles concentrating them in tissues. WHO + global research effort 2020s+.

slides.title: Ecotoxicology: bioaccumulation, biomagnification, LC50, food-web amplification
slides.body:
**Ecotoxicology** (René Truhaut 1969 coined; David Pimentel + Cornell ecological costing) — study of toxicants in ecosystems + non-target organisms. Bridges toxicology + ecology + environmental science.

**Bioaccumulation** — uptake + retention by a single organism over its lifetime. Quantified by **bioconcentration factor (BCF)** = [chemical in organism] / [chemical in water] at steady state. For lipophilic POPs, BCF tracks lipophilicity (logP) + duration of exposure. Highly lipophilic compounds (logP > 5) bioaccumulate intensely.

**Biomagnification** — concentration increases moving up trophic levels. Each predator concentrates contaminants of its prey. For DDT + DDE: water ~10⁻⁹, plankton ~10⁻⁷, small fish ~10⁻⁶, large fish ~10⁻⁵, top predator ~10⁻⁴ — roughly 10× per trophic level + cumulative ~10⁵× from water to apex predator. Why bald eagles + peregrine falcons + osprey crashed under DDT pressure decades after it entered the environment. Same pattern: methylmercury (Minamata + tuna + swordfish + king mackerel — FDA + EPA fish advisories for pregnant women); PCBs (Great Lakes lake trout; cetaceans); PFAS (fish tissue elevated relative to water).

**Aquatic toxicity testing**:
- **LC50 (median lethal concentration)** — concentration killing 50% of test organisms in fixed exposure time. Standard tests: rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss), fathead minnow (Pimephales promelas), Daphnia magna (crustacean), Selenastrum (green alga), zebrafish (Danio rerio embryo). OECD + EPA + ECHA guidelines (TG 203 fish 96-h LC50; TG 202 Daphnia 48-h EC50).
- **Acute vs chronic** — 48-96 h acute vs 21-d Daphnia reproduction or fish early-life-stage. NOEC (No-Observed-Effect Concentration) anchors chronic regulatory limits.
- **Risk quotient** = Predicted Environmental Concentration / Predicted No-Effect Concentration (PEC/PNEC > 1 = unacceptable risk).
- **Species Sensitivity Distribution (SSD)** — fit log-normal to many species' LC50 → derive HC5 (Hazardous Concentration to 5% of species) as community-protective threshold.

**Earthworm + bee + soil + pollinator toxicology**:
- **Earthworm** (Eisenia fetida) — standard soil-toxicity test; integrator of soil contamination.
- **Honey bee + wild bee** — neonicotinoid pesticides (imidacloprid, clothianidin, thiamethoxam) implicated in **colony collapse disorder (CCD)** since 2006-2007 + global pollinator decline (Whitehorn 2012, Henry 2012, Goulson). Neonicotinoids are nAChR agonists in insect CNS; systemic in treated plants (seed coatings persist throughout flowering); chronic sub-lethal effects on bee navigation + foraging + reproduction. EU restricted three neonicotinoids in 2013 + banned outdoor uses 2018; US EPA reviewing.
- **Anguilliforme (eels) + amphibians** — endocrine disruption + parasite loads + population collapse; sentinel species for water quality (Hayes — atrazine in frogs).

**David Pimentel** (Cornell) — pioneered ecological + economic costing of pesticide use; estimated US pesticide externalities (bird + bee + soil + human health) at $5-10B annually vs $35B benefits. Argues true costs offset 'green revolution' yield gains in many cases.

**Modern frameworks**:
- **Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP)** — Ankley + Bradbury 2010+; connects molecular initiating event → key events → adverse outcome at organism + population. AOPwiki (OECD). Used in regulatory + Tox21.
- **Ecological Risk Assessment (ERA)** — EPA framework: problem formulation → analysis (exposure + effects characterization) → risk characterization. Tiered approach.
- **Environmental quality standards (EQS)** — EU Water Framework Directive; numeric standards for priority pollutants.

The central message: toxicants released to environment are not contained; persistence + lipophilicity drive food-chain amplification; ecosystem health + human health are coupled (the One Health framework + Wild's exposome — covered in modern-frontier lesson).

slides.title: Pollutants: PM2.5, lead, arsenic, radon, asbestos, glyphosate, air + water hazards
slides.body:
**Air pollution + PM2.5**:

- **Particulate matter (PM)** — PM10 (coarse), PM2.5 (fine), PM0.1 (ultrafine). PM2.5 (≤2.5 μm aerodynamic diameter) reaches alveoli + deposits there + smallest particles translocate systemically. Sources: combustion (vehicles, power plants, wildfires, cookstoves, residential heating), secondary formation (sulfate + nitrate + SOA from gas-phase precursors), industrial.
- **Pope + Dockery six cities study (Harvard 1993; AJRCCM 2002)** — cohort followup linking PM2.5 to all-cause + cardiopulmonary + lung-cancer mortality. Each 10 μg/m³ PM2.5 → ~4-8% increase in all-cause mortality + ~15% lung-cancer mortality. Foundational evidence underlying US EPA NAAQS revisions (35 μg/m³ 24-h + 9 μg/m³ annual, 2024 revision).
- **Global burden** — ~7 million premature deaths/year attributed to ambient + household air pollution (WHO + GBD). Largest environmental health risk globally. Disproportionate burden in low-income + middle-income countries (LMICs) with household biomass cooking + traffic + industrial.
- **Ozone (O₃, ground-level)** — photochemical secondary; respiratory inflammation + asthma exacerbation + reduced lung function in children. NAAQS 70 ppb 8-h average.
- **NO₂ + SO₂** — primary irritants; NO₂ from combustion (traffic) + power plants. Traffic-related air pollution (TRAP) linked to childhood asthma + COPD.
- **CO** — carbon monoxide; covered in toxicology foundations.

**Lead (Pb)**:
- No safe threshold for children; reference value lowered from 10 → 5 → 3.5 μg/dL (CDC 2021).
- **Aaron Reuben + Duke** longitudinal + ecological studies linking childhood Pb to adult cognition + criminality + mental health.
- Sources: leaded gasoline (US phase-out 1973-1996; Needleman + Bellinger pediatric IQ studies); lead-based paint (banned US 1978; legacy in older housing); lead pipes + solder; industrial; some traditional ceramics + cosmetics; battery recycling in LMICs.
- **Flint Michigan (2014-)** — city switched water source to Flint River without corrosion control; lead leached from pipes; children's blood Pb levels rose; activist Mona Hanna-Attisha + Marc Edwards documented. Iconic environmental-injustice case.
- Universal screening at 12 + 24 months (US AAP); EBLL (elevated blood Pb level) triggers chelation + abatement.

**Arsenic (As)**:
- Naturally occurring + anthropogenic (smelting, pesticides, semiconductor industry, treated wood CCA).
- **Bangladesh tubewells** — 1970s-80s well-drilling program (initially celebrated) inadvertently tapped arsenic-laden aquifers; >50M exposed to As >50 μg/L; arsenicosis + skin lesions + cancer + cardiovascular disease epidemics. **Allan Smith** (UCSF) + Mahfuzar Rahman + national + WHO efforts to identify safe wells + alternative water sources.
- US EPA MCL 10 μg/L. Carcinogenic (IARC Group 1) — skin + lung + bladder + kidney + liver.

**Radon (Rn-222)**:
- Radioactive noble gas from uranium decay; accumulates in homes (basements, crawl spaces, well water).
- Second-leading cause of lung cancer in non-smokers; multiplicative with tobacco. EPA action level 4 pCi/L.
- **Iowa + Sweden case-control studies** (Field + Lubin) confirmed risk at residential levels.

**Asbestos + mesothelioma** — covered in occupational toxicology lesson (Selikoff cohort).

**Glyphosate (Roundup)**:
- Most-used herbicide globally; Monsanto/Bayer (now). Mechanism: inhibits EPSP synthase in shikimate pathway (plants + microbes, not animals).
- **IARC Group 2A (probable carcinogen) 2015** — based on animal + mechanistic data + epidemiological hint of non-Hodgkin lymphoma in agricultural workers. EPA + EFSA + most regulators classify as 'not likely carcinogenic to humans' at typical exposure — conflicting assessments + ongoing controversy.
- **Litigation** — Bayer Roundup lawsuits ~$10B+ settled by 2022; lawn-and-garden formulations reformulated.
- Broader ecological + microbiome concerns: gut microbiome effects (shikimate-pathway organisms), pollinator effects (controversial), aquatic toxicity to amphibians + invertebrates.

**Other ubiquitous pollutants**:
- **Mercury (Hg)** — covered in organ-toxicology (Minamata).
- **VOCs + benzene** — gasoline + solvents; benzene leukemogen (Aksoy Turkish shoemakers; Rinsky NIOSH refinery cohort).
- **Formaldehyde** — embalming + composite-wood off-gassing; nasopharyngeal carcinoma + leukemia.
- **Pesticide drift + residues** — chlorpyrifos developmental neurotoxicity (Eskenazi CHAMACOS; Lanphear; chlorpyrifos US food-use cancellation 2021 then reinstated then re-restricted).
- **Endocrine disruptors in water** — PPCPs (pharmaceuticals + personal-care products), ethinyl estradiol, atrazine.

**Environmental justice** — disproportionate exposure of low-income + minority + indigenous communities (Bullard 1990 'Dumping in Dixie'; EPA EJ 2020 + EJ Index). Concept central to modern environmental health policy.

question.question: Reason through biomagnification of methylmercury through a marine food web
question.goal: A coastal bay has methylmercury water concentration 0.001 μg/L. Plankton bioconcentrate ~10⁴× from water. Small fish (anchovies) eat plankton + concentrate ~5× more. Large predator fish (tuna, swordfish, king mackerel) eat smaller fish + concentrate ~10× more. Compute approximate concentrations at each level + relate to FDA fish-advisory thresholds.

steps.reveal: Plankton: 0.001 μg/L × 10000 = 10 μg/kg (= 0.01 ppm). Reflects equilibrium partitioning of methylmercury (highly lipophilic relative to inorganic Hg²⁺) + protein binding. Inorganic Hg from industrial sources is methylated by sulfate-reducing bacteria in sediments → MeHg enters food web. Minamata: Chisso Chemical discharged inorganic Hg → bay sediment microbes methylated → fish bioaccumulated → human consumers exposed at ~10 ppm fish levels.
Anchovy: 10 μg/kg × 5 = 50 μg/kg (= 0.05 ppm). Within FDA 'safe' range for sushi-grade fish; sardines + anchovies are recommended low-Hg choices.

Tuna/swordfish/king mackerel: 50 × 10 = 500 μg/kg = 0.5 ppm. Approximate FDA action level for fish is 1 ppm; advisories urge pregnant women + young children to avoid tilefish + shark + swordfish + king mackerel + bigeye tuna entirely + limit albacore tuna. FDA + EPA fish advisory (2017) — chart of best choices (salmon, sardines, anchovies, tilapia) vs avoid (high-Hg apex predators). Reflects ~50000× biomagnification from water.

steps.prompt: Why was the Minamata disaster (1956+) so severe?

acceptedAnswers: high direct industrial discharge + heavy reliance on local fish + delayed recognition

steps.reveal: Minamata (Chisso Chemical, Kumamoto Prefecture, 1932-1968 discharge; recognized 1956; >2200 certified victims + many more uncertified): (1) **massive industrial discharge** of inorganic Hg → microbial methylation in bay sediment → MeHg fish levels reached >10 ppm (~20× modern advisory threshold); (2) **heavy reliance on local fish + shellfish** by Minamata fishing community → high cumulative MeHg dose; (3) **delayed recognition + cover-up** by Chisso (denial of responsibility until 1968); (4) **organic methylmercury crosses placenta + BBB** efficiently — congenital Minamata disease (fetal MeHg poisoning; Harada). Paradigm-defining environmental disaster. Drove the **Minamata Convention on Mercury (2013; in force 2017)** — global mercury treaty banning mercury cell chlor-alkali + restricting artisanal gold mining + dental amalgam phaseouts.

question.question: Why is Pope + Dockery's Six Cities + ACS-II cohort study (Harvard 1993, 2002) so consequential for air-pollution regulation?
options: Because it provided robust, prospective cohort evidence linking long-term PM2.5 exposure to cardiopulmonary + lung-cancer + all-cause mortality + quantified the exposure-response (each 10 μg/m³ PM2.5 → ~4-8% increase in all-cause mortality). Independent reanalysis (HEI) confirmed findings. Underpins US EPA NAAQS PM2.5 standards + WHO air quality guidelines + serves as evidence-base for the global air-pollution burden estimate (~7M deaths/yr).
It found PM has no effect.
It applied only to indoor air.
question.explanation: Pope + Dockery + Harvard Six Cities (NEJM 1993; AJRCCM 2002, ACS-II cohort) — prospective cohort linking long-term ambient PM2.5 exposure to: all-cause mortality (HR ~1.04-1.08 per 10 μg/m³); cardiopulmonary mortality; lung-cancer mortality (HR ~1.14 per 10 μg/m³). Findings independently reanalyzed (Health Effects Institute) + replicated in subsequent cohorts (ACS-II, Medicare, ESCAPE European, GBD modeling). Consequences: (i) US EPA PM2.5 NAAQS (1997; revised 2012 to 12 μg/m³; 2024 to 9 μg/m³ annual); (ii) WHO Air Quality Guidelines (2021: 5 μg/m³ annual — most stringent); (iii) global burden of disease attribution (~7M deaths/yr from ambient + household air pollution — leading environmental risk factor; State of Global Air); (iv) drove control-technology investment (selective catalytic reduction, scrubbers, vehicle standards, coal-plant retirements); (v) established epidemiology as policy-relevant in environmental regulation. Modern: low-cost sensors (PurpleAir + others) democratized monitoring + revealed environmental-justice disparities (Bullard) at neighborhood scale.

hints: What was the design + main finding?
What does it underpin in policy?
slides.workedSolution: Pope + Dockery — prospective cohort linking long-term PM2.5 to cardiopulmonary + lung-cancer + all-cause mortality. Each 10 μg/m³ → ~4-8% mortality increase. Independent replication. Underpins EPA NAAQS + WHO AQG + GBD ~7M global deaths/yr. Cornerstone of air-pollution regulation.

question.question: Designing a community response to PFAS-contaminated drinking water
question.prompt: A small US town discovers its public water supply contains PFOA at 30 ppt + PFOS at 50 ppt (well above the EPA MCL of 4 ppt for each). The contamination is traced to a former military base AFFF firefighting training area upgradient. Discuss: (a) the toxicology — what's known about PFOA/PFOS half-lives in humans (3-8 years), targets (developmental, immune via reduced vaccine response per Grandjean's Faroe cohort, thyroid, cholesterol, kidney + testicular cancer), regulatory thresholds; (b) immediate community response — bottled water, point-of-use filters (granular activated carbon, ion exchange), bottled-water distribution, biomonitoring of resident serum PFAS levels via CDC/EPA programs; (c) long-term remediation — replace water source (new wells, surface water, regional connection); treat at the well (GAC, IX, RO); source remediation at the military base (in-situ destruction via supercritical water oxidation or electrochemical methods is emerging); (d) health surveillance — clinical PFAS panel for residents; pediatric immunization-response monitoring; thyroid + lipid + kidney function; tumor surveillance especially testicular + kidney; cohort study; (e) regulatory + legal — EPA MCL + UCMR (unregulated contaminant monitoring rule); litigation against DoD + AFFF manufacturers (3M, DuPont/Chemours, Tyco) following 3M's $10.3B 2023 settlement; (f) equity considerations — environmental-justice analysis since affected communities are disproportionately rural, low-income, indigenous; lessons from Flint MI + Hinkley CA + Anniston AL.

question.question: PFOS has a half-life in humans of 5.4 years. Approximately how many years are needed for serum PFOS to decline 90% after exposure stops (assume first-order elimination)?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) + the Stockholm Convention (2001) + Pope-Dockery PM2.5 epidemiology + Grandjean's PFAS findings reframed environmental toxicology from a 'site-specific contamination' field into a global chemical-safety + public-health discipline.
question.rubric: Mentions: Silent Spring (Carson 1962) — bird population collapse from DDT (eggshell thinning via DDE) + introduced the concept of ecosystem-scale persistent contaminants → led to EPA founding (1970) + DDT ban (1972); Stockholm Convention (2001) — global treaty on POPs (DDT, PCBs, dioxins + furans, aldrin, dieldrin, etc; later additions PFOS, PFOA, PFHxS) with persistence + bioaccumulation + long-range transport + toxicity criteria; Pope-Dockery Six Cities Harvard 1993 + ACS-II 2002 — long-term PM2.5 exposure → cardiopulmonary + cancer mortality at 4-8% per 10 μg/m³ → EPA NAAQS + WHO AQG + global burden ~7M/yr; Grandjean + Weihe Faroe Islands cohort — prenatal PCB + Hg + PFAS exposure → cognitive deficit + reduced vaccine response → developmental immunotoxicity; combined with: Minamata Hg (Harada); Bangladesh As (Smith); microplastics; environmental justice (Bullard). Concludes: environmental toxicology became a population + global discipline integrating chemistry + epidemiology + policy.
